---
title: "Getting started"
description: "Drop EOS Reimagined into a game and get two copies talking over the LAN."
---

EOS Reimagined is a **drop-in replacement** for the EOS SDK's shared library. Running it is a
matter of putting our library where the game already looks for Epic's, then letting the game's own
menus do what they always did.

::: {.callout-important}
## Before you start: the working assumptions

- **Everyone plays on the same LAN.** Peers find each other with a UDP broadcast — same Wi‑Fi
  network or wired subnet. There is no matchmaking server and no Internet traversal yet. Two
  copies on a single machine also work, and are the easiest way to try it.
- **Everyone runs the same game with EOS Reimagined dropped in.** A different game — or the real
  SDK talking to Epic — will not mesh with you, by design.
- **Know what's real and what's stubbed.** The multiplayer and social core is live. Everything
  else — voice, achievements, commerce, anti-cheat — is exported as an *honest stub*: the game
  loads and runs, but those features answer `EOS_NotImplemented` and stay absent. Check the
  [roadmap](roadmap.qmd), and see [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) for how to census a
  specific game before an evening's commitment.
- **You own your copies of the game.** This project exists to keep games playable, not to crack
  them — see [Scope & non-goals](scope.qmd).
:::

## 1. Get the right artifact for the game — not the machine

A game loads the EOS SDK as a shared library, and it keeps loading the same *kind* of library
wherever it runs:

| The game is… | It loads | You want |
|---|---|---|
| A native **Linux** title | `libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so` | the Linux `.so` |
| A **Windows** title on Windows | `EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll` | the Windows `.dll` |
| A **Windows** title under **Proton/Wine** | still the Windows `EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll` | the Windows `.dll` (not the `.so`!) |

Both artifacts build from the same source tree — see [Building from source](building.qmd), or
grab them from a CI run's artifacts if one is available.

## 2. Back up the original

Find the game's existing `EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll` / `libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so` (usually
near the game executable, sometimes under a path like
`<game>/EOSSDK/Bin/`) and rename it — e.g. add a `.orig` suffix — so you can restore Epic's
library when you're done.

## 3. Drop ours in under the same filename

Copy the built library into the same folder, under the exact filename the game shipped Epic's
with. That's the whole install.

```sh
# Example: a native Linux game
cd "/path/to/Game/"
mv libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so.orig
cp ~/EOS-Reimagined/build/libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so .
```

## 4. Give each player an identity

There is nothing to sign up for. On first run the library mints a **profile key** and saves it in
your user data directory; your player identity is derived from that key, and it persists across
runs. The default display name is `Player` — give yourself a real one by creating a small
[`eosr.json`](configuration.qmd) next to your data directory, or with an environment variable:

```sh
EOSR_DISPLAY_NAME="Alice" ./the-game
```

Several copies of the game on one machine each claim their **own profile slot** automatically, so
couch co-op is several distinct players rather than one confused one. To pin a copy's identity
and data to a specific directory (useful for launchers and isolated instances), set
`EOSR_DATA_DIR`. Details in [Identity & profiles](identity-and-profiles.qmd).

## 5. Launch the game and use its own menus

Host a game, or open the game's server/lobby browser, exactly as you would online. Peers running
EOS Reimagined on the same LAN discover each other, complete an authenticated handshake, and show
up to be joined.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quick sanity test: two copies, one machine

1. Install the library into the game (steps above).
2. Start the game twice — two windows. Each instance automatically takes its own discovery port
   and its own profile slot, so they are two different players.
3. In window one, host / create a lobby from the game's menus.
4. In window two, open the game's browser — the hosted game should appear within a few seconds.

If you want the two instances fully isolated (separate saves, names, and configs), point each at
its own data directory instead:

```sh
EOSR_DATA_DIR=~/eosr/p1 EOSR_DISPLAY_NAME=Alice ./the-game &
EOSR_DATA_DIR=~/eosr/p2 EOSR_DISPLAY_NAME=Bob   ./the-game &
```
:::

## If something doesn't work

- The game **exits instantly** or never reaches a menu → you're probably running an old build
  that didn't export the full EOS surface yet. See
  [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd#the-game-wont-launch) — rebuilding usually fixes it, and
  there's a tool that names exactly what's missing.
- The game runs but **a feature does nothing** (voice, achievements, DLC) → that family is an
  honest stub today; see [the roadmap](roadmap.qmd#present-but-not-functional).
- Peers **don't see each other** → same subnet? Firewall allowing UDP 55789–55798? Same game and
  build on both machines? Walk through [Networking & firewalls](networking.qmd).
- Anything else → turn on [tracing](tracing.qmd) and read what the library actually did.
